course.title: CSS
course.description: A complete practical CSS course progressing from syntax, cascade, selectors, and the box model through Flexbox, Grid, responsive and container queries, custom properties, accessibility, motion, debugging, performance, compatibility, and modern positioning. The course culminates in a realistic accessible documentation portal built with platform CSS.
prerequisites: Basic familiarity with HTML elements and document structure
A modern web browser with developer tools
learningOutcomes: Explain CSS syntax, matching, inheritance, cascade, specificity, and layers.
Design maintainable selectors and component boundaries.
Use units, logical properties, box sizing, intrinsic sizing, and CSS math to create predictable dimensions.
Build robust one-dimensional Flexbox and two-dimensional Grid layouts.
Create responsive interfaces with fluid sizing, media queries, container queries, and user preference features.
Build themeable CSS systems with custom properties and semantic tokens.
Implement accessible focus, reduced-motion, forced-colors, color-scheme, and print behavior.
Use transitions, keyframes, and scroll-driven effects as progressive enhancements.
Debug CSS systematically using developer tools and clear hypotheses.
Apply containment and rendering hints cautiously based on real performance needs.
Use feature detection and progressive enhancement for newer CSS capabilities.
Design and implement a production-style CSS architecture in a realistic final project.

modules.title: CSS Foundations and the Cascade
modules.description: Build the mental model needed to understand CSS syntax, declarations, inheritance, cascade, layers, and specificity.

lessons.title: Rules, Declarations, and Values
lessons.description: Learn the grammar of ordinary CSS rules and how declarations are matched to elements.
learningObjectives: identify selectors, properties, values, and declaration blocks

notes.text: A CSS rule combines a selector with a declaration block. Each declaration supplies a property and value. CSS is intentionally error-tolerant: an invalid declaration can be discarded while other valid declarations continue to participate in the stylesheet.

items: A selector determines which elements may match.
A property names the feature being assigned.
A value supplies the requested result and must satisfy that property’s grammar.

practicals.title: Style a semantic article
practicals.description: Apply readable typography and spacing to a semantic article without changing its HTML meaning.
steps: Create an article with a heading, paragraphs, and a list.
Constrain the article measure and center it with logical margins.
Set a readable line-height and heading spacing.
Inspect the result in browser developer tools.
practicals.output: The article becomes a readable, centered content block with consistent spacing.

quiz.question: What identifies the elements to which a declaration block may apply?
quiz.answer: The selector
quiz.explanation: Selectors perform matching; declarations provide property values.

summary: CSS rules are composed from selectors and declarations.
Valid CSS should be debugged with developer tools rather than by guessing.

lessons.title: Inheritance and the Cascade
lessons.description: Understand why one declaration wins when multiple declarations can style the same property.
learningObjectives: describe the main cascade decision stages
use inherit, initial, unset, and revert intentionally

notes.text: The cascade is a conflict-resolution algorithm. Relevance is considered first, then origin and importance, cascade layer precedence, specificity, scoping proximity where applicable, and source order. Inheritance supplies values when an inherited property has no closer winning declaration.

items: Specificity is not the first decision in the cascade.
Custom properties inherit by default.
`revert-layer` can hand a declaration back to an earlier cascade layer.

quiz.question: Which is considered before specificity in the cascade?
quiz.answer: Origin and importance
quiz.explanation: Specificity is compared after the applicable origin/importance and layer precedence have been resolved.

summary: Inheritance is property-specific.
Cascade layers can reduce specificity escalation.

lessons.title: Specificity and Selector Strategy
lessons.description: Calculate common specificity relationships and design selectors that remain easy to override.

notes.text: Specificity is compared among declarations that have already survived the higher-precedence cascade decisions. `:where()` contributes zero specificity, while `:is()` takes the specificity of its most specific argument.

:where(.card) h2 { margin-block-end: .5rem; }
:is(.card, #featured) h2 { color: currentColor; }

items: Prefer stable class contracts for components.
Avoid encoding page ancestry into reusable selectors.
Use low specificity as an architectural choice.

quiz.question: What is special about :where()?
quiz.answer: Its argument contributes zero specificity
quiz.explanation: The selectors inside `:where()` contribute zero specificity.

summary: Specificity is a tie-breaker inside an already-selected cascade context.
Low-specificity CSS is easier to evolve.

lessons.title: Cascade Layers and Native Nesting
lessons.description: Use modern CSS architecture features to express precedence and component ownership.

notes.text: Cascade layers create named precedence groups. Native nesting reduces repeated selectors. `@scope` limits matching to a DOM subtree and can reduce coupling to global structure.

items: Layer order should be established deliberately.
Nesting is CSS syntax, not inherently a preprocessor feature.
Scoped styling is useful when a component should not affect unrelated subtrees.

quiz.question: What is a primary purpose of cascade layers?
options: To make precedence between style groups explicit
quiz.answer: To make precedence between style groups explicit
quiz.explanation: Layers provide named, ordered buckets in the cascade.

summary: Layers make precedence explicit.
Nesting can reduce repetition without increasing page coupling.

tasks.title: Replace a specificity escalation chain
tasks.description: Refactor deeply nested component rules into a predictable layer and component contract.
tasks.problemStatement: A button can only be overridden with increasingly specific page selectors. Rebuild the styling with layers and a root component class.
hint: Start from the component boundary and make precedence explicit.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The component owns its styles and the utility layer provides a deliberate override without selector escalation.

modules.title: Box Model, Values, Sizing, and Overflow
modules.description: Learn units, logical properties, box sizing, intrinsic sizing, overflow, and CSS math.

lessons.title: Units and Logical Properties
lessons.description: Choose units according to the relationship a value should have to its context.
learningObjectives: distinguish rem, em, percentages, viewport units, and logical units

notes.text: `rem` is based on the root font size; `em` is relative to the relevant font size. Viewport units relate to viewport dimensions, while logical properties and units follow the writing-mode axes.

items: Use logical properties for reusable internationalized components.
Use viewport units as part of a constraint system, not as a replacement for content sizing.

quiz.question: Which unit is based on the root element font size?
quiz.answer: rem
quiz.explanation: `rem` is relative to the root element’s computed font size.

summary: Unit choice expresses a relationship.
Logical properties reduce left/right assumptions.

lessons.title: The Box Model and box-sizing
lessons.description: Predict dimensions and spacing using content, padding, border, and margin.

notes.text:
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
.card { inline-size: 20rem; padding: 1rem; border: 2px solid; }

With `border-box`, the specified size includes content, padding, and border. Margin is outside the border. Vertical margins can collapse in certain block formatting situations, which is distinct from padding and border spacing.

practicals.title: Make card dimensions predictable
practicals.description: Use border-box sizing so padding and borders do not unexpectedly expand a declared card size.
steps: Apply border-box to elements and pseudo-elements.
Create a card with a constrained inline size, padding, and border.
Inspect the box model in developer tools.
Change padding and verify the declared outer size remains bounded.
practicals.solution:
*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
.card { inline-size: min(100%, 22rem); padding: 1rem; border: 2px solid; }
practicals.output: The card’s declared size includes its padding and border.

quiz.question: What does border-box include in the declared size?
quiz.answer: Content, padding, and border
quiz.explanation: The border-box sizing model includes content, padding, and border in the specified size.

summary: Border-box makes declared dimensions easier to reason about.
Margin collapse is context-dependent.

lessons.title: Intrinsic Sizing and Overflow
lessons.description: Prevent content from forcing brittle fixed-size layouts.

notes.text: Intrinsic sizing lets content contribute to an element’s dimensions. Constraints bound that contribution. Flex and grid items can retain automatic minimum sizes, so `min-inline-size: 0` is often an important escape hatch for long content.

items: Constrain replaced elements such as images.
Give code or long data an intentional overflow policy.
Do not hide overflow globally just to make a symptom disappear.

quiz.question: Why can min-inline-size: 0 help a flex/grid child?
options: It allows the item to shrink below an automatic minimum
It fixes the item at zero width
quiz.answer: It allows the item to shrink below an automatic minimum
quiz.explanation: Flex/grid automatic minimum sizing can otherwise prevent a content column from shrinking enough.

summary: Intrinsic sizing is a major part of responsive design.
Overflow should be handled at the component that owns it.

lessons.title: CSS Math with min, max, clamp, and calc
lessons.description: Build fluid constraints without a large breakpoint matrix.
learningObjectives: use clamp for bounded fluid values

notes.text: `min()` selects the smallest candidate, `max()` selects the largest, and `clamp()` bounds a preferred value between a minimum and maximum. These functions are useful for fluid typography, spacing, and container constraints.

quiz.question: Which function bounds a preferred value between a minimum and maximum?
quiz.answer: clamp()
quiz.explanation: `clamp(min, preferred, max)` returns a value bounded by its minimum and maximum.

summary: Math functions can reduce breakpoint dependence.
Always test the resulting values at intermediate sizes.

tasks.title: Build a fluid reading shell
tasks.description: Create a documentation shell that stays readable from phone to desktop widths.
tasks.problemStatement: Use a bounded container, fluid heading, logical spacing, and no horizontal overflow.
hint: Let content define the minimum; let the viewport supply the available maximum.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The shell grows fluidly but remains bounded, while the article and media avoid runaway widths.

modules.title: Typography, Color, Backgrounds, and Themes
modules.description: Build readable and coherent visual systems with modern color functions, typography controls, and system-aware themes.

lessons.title: Typography and Text Layout
lessons.description: Control font stacks, line-height, measure, wrapping, and hierarchy.

notes.text: Typography depends on font metrics, size, line height, language, and measure. A resilient stylesheet avoids assuming a particular font will always be available or have identical metrics.

quiz.question: Why should a font stack include fallbacks?
options: The preferred font may be unavailable
They remove the need for font loading
quiz.answer: The preferred font may be unavailable
quiz.explanation: A fallback stack gives the browser usable alternatives when the preferred face is unavailable.

summary: Typography must be tested with real content.
Readable measure is often more important than maximizing line length.

lessons.title: Modern CSS Color
lessons.description: Use color spaces and functions while keeping accessibility in view.
learningObjectives: use rgb/hsl and modern color spaces
understand that color choice must be checked in context

notes.text: CSS supports sRGB functions as well as Lab, LCH, OKLab, OKLCH, relative colors, and mixing functions. The color model affects interpolation and the resulting appearance, but accessibility still depends on the final colors and their context.

quiz.question: Which function combines colors in a chosen interpolation color space?
quiz.answer: color-mix()
quiz.explanation: `color-mix()` mixes colors using the specified interpolation space.

summary: Color functions enable systematic palettes.
Never treat color alone as the only state indicator.

lessons.title: Backgrounds, Borders, Radius, and Shadows
lessons.description: Compose surfaces and hierarchy without using decoration as structural layout.
learningObjectives: apply shadows as supporting visual cues

notes.text: Multiple backgrounds are layered in order. Borders participate in layout; outlines are painted outside the border and are commonly useful for focus indicators. Shadows can communicate elevation but should not be the only way to convey important boundaries.

quiz.question: Which background layer is closest to the user?
quiz.answer: The first listed layer
quiz.explanation: The first listed background layer is painted closest to the user.

summary: Background layers are visual composition tools.
Focus indicators should not depend on subtle shadows alone.

lessons.title: Color Scheme and light-dark()
lessons.description: Support user light/dark preferences and browser-provided UI colors.

notes.text: `color-scheme` communicates supported schemes to the user agent and can affect browser UI such as form controls. `light-dark()` chooses between two values based on the used color scheme in supporting browsers.

practicals.title: Build a system-aware theme
practicals.description: Use color-scheme and light-dark() to create semantic light and dark surface tokens.
steps: Declare supported color schemes on :root.
Create surface and text custom properties with light-dark().
Use the tokens on the page and a card.
Switch the browser color-scheme preference and inspect the result.
practicals.output: The semantic tokens resolve to different values when the active color scheme changes.

quiz.question: What does color-scheme communicate?
options: Which color schemes the UI supports
quiz.answer: Which color schemes the UI supports
quiz.explanation: The property informs the user agent about supported light/dark schemes and affects relevant browser UI.

summary: Themes should be token-driven.
Dark mode is a separate contrast and surface design problem, not a simple inversion.

tasks.title: Create a semantic theme foundation
tasks.description: Build a small light/dark token system for a reusable component library.
tasks.problemStatement: Define surface, text, muted, border, accent, and focus tokens and use them without duplicating the component stylesheet for each theme.
hint: Name tokens by role, not by literal color.
tasks.solutionExplanation: Semantic roles let the visual values change without rewriting component structure.

modules.title: Normal Flow, Positioning, and Layering
modules.description: Understand normal flow, containing blocks, positioned layout, stacking contexts, and logical axes.

lessons.title: Normal Flow and Formatting Contexts
lessons.description: Use normal flow as the default layout model and understand when formatting contexts change behavior.

notes.text:
.stack { display: flow-root; }
.stack > * + * { margin-block-start: 1rem; }

Normal flow lays out content according to the document formatting model. Flex and grid create their own layout contexts. `display: flow-root` establishes a new block formatting context and can isolate certain float and margin interactions.

quiz.question: Why might display: flow-root be useful?
options: To establish a new block formatting context
quiz.answer: To establish a new block formatting context
quiz.explanation: A new block formatting context can isolate layout effects such as floats and margin behavior.

summary: Prefer flow and layout systems before positioning hacks.
Formatting contexts are a diagnostic tool as well as a layout mechanism.

lessons.title: Positioned Layout
lessons.description: Use relative, absolute, fixed, and sticky positioning with explicit containing-block relationships.
learningObjectives: build local overlays and sticky UI

notes.text: Absolute positioning removes an element from normal flow and positions it relative to its containing block. Sticky positioning remains in flow and becomes offset within its scroll context when its threshold is reached.

practicals.title: Build a local badge overlay
practicals.description: Position a badge relative to its card instead of the page.
steps: Make the card a positioned ancestor.
Create a badge element.
Position the badge with logical inset properties.
Resize and move the card to verify the badge follows it.
practicals.solution:
.card { position: relative; }
.badge { position: absolute; inset-block-start: .75rem; inset-inline-end: .75rem; }
practicals.output: The badge stays attached to the card’s corner while the card moves.

quiz.question: What common declaration establishes a containing block for an absolutely positioned child?
quiz.answer: position: relative
quiz.explanation: A positioned ancestor such as `position: relative` commonly establishes the containing block for an absolute descendant.

summary: Position overlays relative to a component boundary.
Sticky behavior depends on the scroll container and inset threshold.

lessons.title: Stacking Contexts and z-index
lessons.description: Debug layering by understanding stacking contexts rather than escalating numbers.

notes.text: `z-index` does not create one global ordering across the entire page. Stacking contexts are nested painting contexts. A descendant cannot escape the overall stacking order of its ancestor context.

.overlay { position: fixed; inset: 0; z-index: 1000; }
.modal { position: relative; z-index: 1; }

items: Transforms and certain opacity/containment configurations can create stacking contexts.
When z-index appears ineffective, inspect ancestors first.

quiz.question: Why can a huge z-index still lose?
options: Its ancestor stacking context may be below another context
quiz.answer: Its ancestor stacking context may be below another context
quiz.explanation: Nested stacking contexts constrain how descendants can be ordered relative to outside contexts.

summary: Layering bugs are usually structural.
Keep a deliberate small z-index scale.

lessons.title: Logical Layout and Writing Modes
lessons.description: Write reusable layout rules that follow block and inline axes.
learningObjectives: use logical spacing and inset properties

notes.text: .card { padding-block: 1rem; padding-inline: 1.25rem; margin-inline: auto; border-inline-start: .25rem solid currentColor; }
Logical properties describe the relationship to the current writing mode. They are valuable for reusable components because the same CSS can adapt to right-to-left and non-horizontal writing modes.

quiz.question: What axis does margin-inline affect?
quiz.answer: The inline axis
quiz.explanation: Logical inline properties follow the document’s inline axis.

summary: Logical properties encode intent.
Use them consistently inside component systems.

tasks.title: Repair a broken modal layer
tasks.description: Fix a modal that remains behind a transformed application shell.
tasks.problemStatement: The modal has a large z-index but is still visually behind the app. Move the overlay into an appropriate stacking context and remove unnecessary context creation.
objectives: place overlay at a suitable level
hint: Inspect stacking contexts before changing numbers.
tasks.solutionCode:
.overlay { position: fixed; inset: 0; z-index: 1000; }
.modal { position: relative; z-index: 1; }
tasks.solutionExplanation: The overlay participates in a top-level context rather than trying to escape a lower ancestor stacking context.

modules.title: Flexbox
modules.description: Master one-dimensional flexible layout, free-space distribution, alignment, wrapping, and common component patterns.

lessons.title: Flex Container and Axes
lessons.description: Understand main/cross axes, direction, wrapping, and gaps.

notes.text: .toolbar { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; gap: .75rem; align-items: center; }

Flexbox is one-dimensional: items are arranged along a main axis and aligned on a cross axis. The axes depend on flex-direction and writing mode, so they should not be memorized as horizontal and vertical.

quiz.question: What determines the flex main axis?
quiz.answer: flex-direction and the writing mode
quiz.explanation: The main axis follows the flex direction in the current writing mode.

summary: Think in logical axes.
Flexbox is excellent for toolbars, navigation, and local component arrangements.

lessons.title: Flex Sizing and the flex Shorthand
lessons.description: Understand basis, growth, shrinkage, and automatic minimum sizing.

notes.text:
.sidebar { flex: 0 1 18rem; }
.content { flex: 1 1 auto; min-inline-size: 0; }

The flexing algorithm starts from flex base sizes and resolves free space using grow or shrink factors. Automatic minimum sizes can prevent content columns from shrinking, which is why `min-inline-size: 0` is a common fix.

quiz.question: Why is min-inline-size: 0 often added to a flex content column?
options: To allow it to shrink below its automatic minimum
quiz.answer: To allow it to shrink below its automatic minimum
quiz.explanation: The automatic minimum size can otherwise keep long content from shrinking enough.

summary: Flexbox distributes space algorithmically.
Inspect basis and minimum size before forcing widths.

lessons.title: Alignment and Auto Margins
lessons.description: Use alignment properties and auto margins to express layout intent.
learningObjectives: use auto margins for asymmetric groups

notes.text:
.nav { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 1rem; }
.nav__account { margin-inline-start: auto; }
Auto margins can absorb free space on a flex axis. This often gives a clean way to push a control group to an edge without adding spacer elements.

practicals.title: Split a navigation bar
practicals.description: Use an auto margin to push account actions to the inline end of a flex navigation bar.
steps: Create a flex navigation container.
Add a group of primary links.
Add an account link after the primary links.
Apply an inline-start auto margin to the account link.
practicals.solution:
.nav { display: flex; flex-wrap: wrap; align-items: center; gap: 1rem; }
.nav__account { margin-inline-start: auto; }
practicals.output: When space permits, the account action is pushed to the inline end without a spacer element.

quiz.question: What can margin-inline-start:auto do in a flex row?
options: Absorb free space and push an item toward the inline end
Set the item to fixed width
quiz.answer: Absorb free space and push an item toward the inline end
quiz.explanation: Auto margins absorb available free space along the relevant axis.

summary: Alignment properties describe groups.
Auto margins are useful when one group should consume remaining space.

lessons.title: Responsive Flex Patterns
lessons.description: Build media objects and toolbars that survive changing content.

notes.text: A robust flex component gives content permission to wrap and shrink. Fixed heights are especially risky for text-heavy components.

quiz.question: When is Grid usually a better primary layout model than Flexbox?
options: When independent row and column relationships matter
quiz.answer: When independent row and column relationships matter
quiz.explanation: Grid is designed for two-dimensional track-based layout.

summary: Use Flexbox for one-dimensional relationships.
When both row and column tracks must align independently, consider Grid.

tasks.title: Build a resilient media card
tasks.description: Create a media component that wraps naturally without fixed heights.
tasks.problemStatement: A card contains an image, title, metadata, description, and action and must remain readable in narrow containers.
hint: Give the text column a flexible basis and zero automatic minimum.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The image has a bounded basis and the text column can shrink and wrap without forcing overflow.

modules.title: CSS Grid and Subgrid
modules.description: Build two-dimensional layouts, responsive card grids, named areas, and cross-component alignment.

lessons.title: Grid Tracks and Lines
lessons.description: Use explicit tracks, line placement, gaps, and fractional sizing.

notes.text:
.layout { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 16rem minmax(0, 1fr); gap: 2rem; }
.main { grid-column: 2; }
Grid tracks are rows or columns. Grid lines surround those tracks and provide placement coordinates. The `fr` unit distributes flexible space after other track contributions are resolved.

quiz.question: What does 1fr represent in a grid track?
options: A fraction of available flexible space
quiz.answer: A fraction of available flexible space
quiz.explanation: `fr` distributes flexible space among tracks after other contributions are considered.

summary: Grid is two-dimensional.
Use minmax(0,1fr) for content columns that must be allowed to shrink.

lessons.title: Responsive Grids with minmax and auto-fit
lessons.description: Create card grids that respond to available width without device breakpoints.

notes.text: .cards { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 16rem), 1fr)); gap: 1rem; }
`minmax()` supplies lower and upper sizing limits. `auto-fit` can collapse empty repeated tracks and allow existing items to expand, producing a useful content-driven grid.

practicals.title: Create an auto-fitting card grid
practicals.description: Build a responsive grid that changes its column count according to available width.
steps: Create a grid container.
Use repeat(auto-fit, minmax(...)).
Add a consistent gap.
Resize the viewport and an enclosing container.
practicals.output: Cards form as many columns as the available width can support without requiring device-specific breakpoints.

quiz.question: What does minmax(16rem,1fr) provide?
quiz.answer: A 16rem minimum and flexible maximum
quiz.explanation: The track has a lower bound and can grow flexibly.

summary: Responsive grids should be tested at intermediate widths.
Container width, not device identity, should determine card fit.

lessons.title: Named Grid Areas
lessons.description: Express a page shell as readable regions.

notes.text: Named areas make the relationship between semantic regions and layout visible in the stylesheet. They are useful for stable page shells.

quiz.question: What is the main benefit of named grid areas?
quiz.answer: They make page-region relationships explicit
quiz.explanation: Named areas create a readable mapping between semantic regions and grid placement.

summary: Named areas improve readability for page-level layout.
Repeated content usually benefits from auto-placement instead of manual coordinates.

lessons.title: Subgrid for Shared Alignment
lessons.description: Use parent tracks inside nested components when repeated content must align.

notes.text:
.cards { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); gap: 1rem; }
.card { display: grid; grid-template-rows: subgrid; grid-row: span 3; }
Subgrid allows a nested grid to participate in its parent’s track sizing. It is particularly useful for repeated cards whose titles, bodies, and actions need cross-card alignment.

quiz.question: What does subgrid allow?
options: A nested grid to use its parent grid tracks
A grid to become a flex container
quiz.answer: A nested grid to use its parent grid tracks
quiz.explanation: Subgrid exposes parent tracks to the nested grid for alignment.

summary: Subgrid is about shared track sizing, not simply shorter CSS.
Guard optional enhancements with feature detection when compatibility requires it.

tasks.title: Build a responsive dashboard shell
tasks.description: Create a two-dimensional dashboard with adaptive metric cards.
tasks.problemStatement: Use Grid for the page shell and auto-fit/minmax for metrics. Where useful, use subgrid for repeated card alignment.
hint: Separate page-shell layout from repeated card layout.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The page shell and repeated card system respond independently to available space.

modules.title: Responsive Design and Container Queries
modules.description: Design around available space, user preferences, and component context rather than device labels.

lessons.title: Mobile-First Media Queries
lessons.description: Use breakpoints when the current layout fails, not because a device has a particular name.

notes.text: @media (width >= 48rem) { .page { grid-template-columns: 16rem minmax(0,1fr); } }
A mobile-first stylesheet starts with a usable narrow baseline and adds layout changes when available space makes them useful. Breakpoints should be discovered from content and layout constraints.

quiz.question: What is a durable reason to add a breakpoint?
options: The current layout no longer works at that width
Every page should have three breakpoints
quiz.answer: The current layout no longer works at that width
quiz.explanation: Content and layout constraints are more stable than device names.

summary: Breakpoints are layout decisions.
Test between named widths, not only at them.

lessons.title: User Preference Media Features
lessons.description: Respect reduced motion, color scheme, pointer, contrast, and related preferences.

notes.text: Media queries can evaluate user preferences and device capabilities. Reduced motion is especially important for decorative transitions and animations. Forced colors is an accessibility environment that should generally be respected rather than overridden.

quiz.question: Which media feature detects a request for less motion?
quiz.answer: prefers-reduced-motion
quiz.explanation: The feature exposes the user’s reduced-motion preference.

summary: Preference queries adapt the experience, not just the geometry.
Do not hide essential meaning when motion is removed.

lessons.title: Container Queries and Container Units
lessons.description: Make reusable components respond to their own containing context.
learningObjectives: use cqi and related units appropriately

notes.text:
.card-region { container-type: inline-size; }
@container (width >= 36rem) { .card { grid-template-columns: 12rem minmax(0,1fr); } }

Container queries evaluate conditions against a query container rather than the viewport. This makes components portable across sidebars, grids, and main content areas. Container query length units such as `cqi` are relative to the query container’s inline size.

practicals.title: Make a component container-aware
practicals.description: Use a query container and @container so a card changes layout based on its own available width.
steps: Create a wrapper around the card.
Set container-type: inline-size on the wrapper.
Write a container query for a wide card state.
Resize the wrapper independently of the viewport.
practicals.output: The card switches layout when its containing region becomes wide enough.

quiz.question: What does a container query evaluate?
options: A query container’s size or condition
quiz.answer: A query container’s size or condition
quiz.explanation: Container queries make component behavior depend on its containing context.

summary: Container queries solve component-level responsive problems.
Media queries remain useful for page-level or environment-level conditions.

lessons.title: Print and Responsive Delivery
lessons.description: Adapt CSS to print and understand the boundary between image resource selection and presentation.
learningObjectives: distinguish HTML responsive image selection from CSS display sizing

notes.text: CSS can target print media and the `@page` rule can influence printed page properties. HTML features such as `srcset` and `sizes` select image resources; CSS controls how the chosen resource is displayed.

quiz.question: Which at-rule targets print presentation?
quiz.answer: @media print
quiz.explanation: `@media print` applies CSS rules for print media.

summary: Print is a real output medium.
Essential information should remain in document content rather than decorative backgrounds.

tasks.title: Make a reusable card container-aware
tasks.description: Use container queries so the same component works in a sidebar and main content.
tasks.problemStatement: The card is stacked in narrow containers and becomes a two-column media layout when its own container is wide enough.
hint: Ask which box actually controls the card’s available width.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The card adapts to its container and remains reusable in different page contexts.

modules.title: Custom Properties and CSS Architecture
modules.description: Create scalable CSS with semantic tokens, component contracts, layers, nesting, and scoped styling.

lessons.title: Custom Properties and var()
lessons.description: Use custom properties as runtime-resolved CSS values.

notes.text:
:root { --space-4: 1rem; --radius-card: .75rem; }
.card { padding: var(--space-4); border-radius: var(--radius-card); }
Custom properties participate in the cascade and inherit by default. `var()` substitutes them at computed-value time. They can therefore form theme values and component inputs without a build step.

quiz.question: What is a notable property of custom properties?
options: They participate in the cascade and normally inherit
quiz.answer: They participate in the cascade and normally inherit
quiz.explanation: Custom properties are CSS declarations that participate in cascading and inheritance.

summary: Custom properties are part of the cascade.
Choose semantic names when the value represents a role.

lessons.title: Semantic Tokens and Component APIs
lessons.description: Separate design roles from literal implementation values.

notes.text:
:root { --color-surface: #fff; --color-text: #0f172a; --color-accent: #075985; }
.button { --button-bg: var(--color-accent); background: var(--button-bg); }

A semantic token names a purpose such as surface, text, accent, or focus. Component variables can form a deliberate customization API while hiding internal implementation details that consumers should not depend on.

quiz.question: Why is --color-accent often better than --blue-600 as a public token?
options: It describes role rather than implementation
quiz.answer: It describes role rather than implementation
quiz.explanation: Semantic names allow the underlying color to change without renaming consumers.

summary: Token names are an API design decision.
Avoid exposing every private implementation value.

lessons.title: Layered CSS Architecture
lessons.description: Use reset, base, component, utility, and override layers deliberately.

notes.text: Layers let a stylesheet encode architectural precedence. Once the layer order is defined, selector specificity does not need to carry the entire burden of maintainability.

quiz.question: What do cascade layers primarily organize?
options: Precedence between groups of author styles
quiz.answer: Precedence between groups of author styles
quiz.explanation: Layers create named, ordered groups in the cascade.

summary: Layers reduce accidental precedence fights.
Define the layer order early.

lessons.title: Nesting and Scoped Component Styles
lessons.description: Combine native nesting with @scope to keep component CSS local and readable.

notes.text: Nesting expresses relationships close to the root selector. `@scope` limits where a style can match and can make a component boundary explicit without relying on very specific descendant chains.

quiz.question: What is @scope designed to do?
options: Limit style matching to a DOM subtree
quiz.answer: Limit style matching to a DOM subtree
quiz.explanation: `@scope` establishes a scoped styling context for selectors.

summary: Nesting is useful when it clarifies ownership.
Scope can reduce global selector coupling.

tasks.title: Create a maintainable component system
tasks.description: Build a small token and layer foundation for buttons and cards.
tasks.problemStatement: The system must support themes, focus states, utilities, and component ownership without deep page selectors.
hint: Treat tokens and layers as APIs with explicit contracts.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The system establishes explicit precedence and a small public component surface.

modules.title: Motion, Accessibility, and UI States
modules.description: Use transitions and animations responsibly while preserving focus, reduced-motion, forced-colors, and native-control usability.

lessons.title: Transitions and Transforms
lessons.description: Animate state changes without making layout depend on motion.
learningObjectives: animate transform and opacity for common effects

notes.text:
.button { transition: transform 160ms ease, background-color 160ms ease; }
.button:hover { transform: translateY(-1px); }
A transition describes interpolation when a property value changes. It does not create the state change. Transforms can often provide motion without changing layout geometry.

quiz.question: What does a transition define?
options: How a property change is interpolated over time
quiz.answer: How a property change is interpolated over time
quiz.explanation: Transitions describe the interpolation between computed values.

summary: Motion should communicate interaction.
Keep decorative motion short and optional.

lessons.title: Keyframes and Animation Control
lessons.description: Build multi-step animations with explicit timing and iteration.

notes.text:
@keyframes pulse { 0%,100% { transform: scale(1); } 50% { transform: scale(1.04); } }
.badge { animation: pulse 1.6s ease-in-out infinite; }
Keyframes define stages of an animation. Animation properties control duration, timing, delay, iteration, direction, fill behavior, and play state.

quiz.question: Where are animation stages declared?
quiz.answer: @keyframes
quiz.explanation: `@keyframes` defines the property values at stages of a CSS animation.

summary: Avoid infinite motion unless it has a clear purpose.
Provide reduced-motion behavior for non-essential animation.

lessons.title: Focus, Keyboard States, and Forced Colors
lessons.description: Preserve visible interaction cues across input methods and system color environments.

notes.text:
button:focus-visible, a:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid Highlight; outline-offset: 3px; }
@media (forced-colors: active) { .custom-control { border: 1px solid ButtonText; } }

Keyboard users need a visible focus indicator. Forced-colors mode can replace author colors with a restricted palette, so authors should generally preserve that mode and make only targeted adjustments where necessary.

items: Do not remove native focus without a replacement.
Do not use color as the sole representation of validation or state.
System colors such as Highlight and ButtonText can integrate custom UI with forced-color palettes.

practicals.title: Add accessible focus states
practicals.description: Provide visible focus for keyboard users while using system-friendly colors.
steps: Create a link and button.
Add :focus-visible styling with a visible outline.
Do not remove the native focus indicator without replacement.
Test using only the keyboard.
practicals.output: Keyboard navigation produces a clear focus indicator.

quiz.question: What is the recommended approach to forced-colors mode?
options: Respect the user’s restricted palette and make targeted usability fixes
quiz.answer: Respect the user’s restricted palette and make targeted usability fixes
quiz.explanation: Forced colors exists to improve accessibility; authors should avoid fighting the system palette.

summary: Focus is an interaction requirement.
Forced colors is an accessibility environment, not a theme to override.

lessons.title: Reduced Motion and Scroll-Driven Effects
lessons.description: Use scroll-driven animation as an enhancement with an accessible baseline.

notes.text: Scroll-driven animations tie keyframes to scroll or view progress rather than elapsed time. The baseline should remain visible and usable even when the feature is unsupported or motion is reduced.

quiz.question: What drives a scroll-driven animation?
options: A scroll or view progress timeline
quiz.answer: A scroll or view progress timeline
quiz.explanation: The animation timeline is linked to scroll or element visibility progress.

summary: Progressive motion should never hide essential content.
Use feature detection for newer animation capabilities.

tasks.title: Harden an interactive component
tasks.description: Audit and repair focus, reduced-motion, and forced-colors behavior.
tasks.problemStatement: A card has hover-only feedback and a decorative infinite animation. Make it usable by keyboard users and people who request reduced motion.
hint: Make the static state correct first, then enhance it.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The component remains fully usable without motion and provides a visible keyboard focus state.

modules.title: Debugging, Performance, Compatibility, and Modern CSS
modules.description: Develop a production workflow for diagnosing CSS, optimizing measured bottlenecks, and adopting newer platform features responsibly.

lessons.title: Systematic CSS Debugging
lessons.description: Turn a visual symptom into a testable CSS hypothesis.
learningObjectives: use computed styles and box-model tools
separate cascade, sizing, layout, and rendering problems

items: Confirm the actual element and state.
Inspect matched rules and the winning declaration.
Check computed and inherited values.
Inspect layout overlays and box metrics.
Trace containing blocks and stacking contexts for positioned UI.
Change one hypothesis at a time.

notes.text: Do not respond to every conflict with !important or every overflow with overflow-x:hidden. Find the actual cause first.

practicals.title: Diagnose an overflow bug
practicals.description: Use developer tools to identify the actual source of horizontal overflow instead of hiding it globally.
steps: Inspect the document scrollable width.
Check flex/grid children for automatic minimum sizes.
Check images for unconstrained dimensions.
Check long unbroken text or code.
Apply the smallest fix that addresses the source.
practicals.output: The component becomes able to shrink or scroll the specific content that requires it, without globally hiding page overflow.

quiz.question: What is a strong first step when a declaration appears not to work?
options: Inspect whether it is matched, valid, and winning
quiz.answer: Inspect whether it is matched, valid, and winning
quiz.explanation: Developer tools can distinguish selector, syntax, cascade, and computed-value problems.

summary: Developer tools make CSS debugging observable.
Debug by category instead of random property changes.

lessons.title: Containment, content-visibility, and will-change
lessons.description: Use rendering optimizations only when they address real costs.
learningObjectives: use content-visibility for suitable offscreen content

notes.text: .article-section { content-visibility: auto; contain-intrinsic-size: auto 600px; }

Containment can limit how changes propagate through layout and painting. `content-visibility:auto` allows suitable offscreen content to defer rendering work. `will-change` is a rendering hint and should be used sparingly for known changes rather than as a generic speed flag.

quiz.question: What is a suitable use of content-visibility:auto?
options: Large offscreen sections whose rendering can be deferred
Essential content that must always render immediately
quiz.answer: Large offscreen sections whose rendering can be deferred
quiz.explanation: The property can allow browsers to skip rendering work for offscreen content until needed.

summary: Performance optimization should follow measurement.
Overusing will-change can increase resource use and create worse performance.

lessons.title: Progressive Enhancement and @supports
lessons.description: Adopt newer CSS without making essential functionality depend on it.
learningObjectives: distinguish specification status from target-browser support

notes.text:
.card { display: flex; gap: 1rem; }
@supports (grid-template-rows: subgrid) { .card { display: grid; grid-template-rows: subgrid; } }

Progressive enhancement starts from a working baseline and adds capabilities when supported. A feature can be standardized while still having incomplete support in the browsers a product targets, so compatibility data and testing matter.

quiz.question: What does @supports provide?
options: CSS feature detection for conditional rules
quiz.answer: CSS feature detection for conditional rules
quiz.explanation: `@supports` conditionally applies CSS based on feature support.

summary: Fallbacks should preserve content and task completion.
Feature detection is better than guessing from browser names.

lessons.title: Anchor Positioning
lessons.description: Use modern anchor positioning for UI that must remain tethered to a trigger.
learningObjectives: use anchor() for relative offsets and understand support limits

notes.text:
.trigger { anchor-name: --trigger; }
.tooltip { position: fixed; position-anchor: --trigger; inset-block-start: anchor(bottom); inset-inline-start: anchor(start); }

Anchor positioning lets a positioned element be associated with an anchor element and positioned or sized relative to it. It is suited to tooltips, popovers, and other tethered UI where ordinary fixed offsets become fragile.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of anchor positioning?
options: Tether a positioned element to an anchor element
quiz.answer: Tether a positioned element to an anchor element
quiz.explanation: Anchor positioning provides CSS mechanisms for associating and positioning one element relative to another.

summary: Anchor positioning is a newer platform capability.
Provide a functional fallback for critical UI when target support requires it.

tasks.title: Perform a production CSS audit
tasks.description: Refactor a component for cascade, responsiveness, accessibility, and performance readiness.
tasks.problemStatement: The component has deep selectors, fixed widths, missing focus styles, and an unnecessary will-change declaration. Produce a production-ready stylesheet.
hint: Audit by cascade, sizing, interaction, accessibility, performance, and compatibility.
tasks.solutionExplanation: The refactoring addresses actual maintainability and usability problems while treating newer CSS as progressive enhancement.

modules.title: Final Project: Accessible Responsive Documentation Portal
modules.description: Build a realistic CSS-only documentation portal combining cascade architecture, responsive layout, themes, accessibility, and progressive enhancement.

lessons.title: Project Architecture and Requirements
lessons.description: Plan the final portal before writing CSS so each platform feature has a clear purpose.

notes.text: The final project is an accessible documentation portal with a global header, sidebar navigation, article content, callouts, related links, and footer. It must support narrow and wide layouts, system color schemes, visible keyboard focus, reduced motion, print, and progressive enhancement.

items: Grid owns page-level two-dimensional relationships.
Flexbox owns local navigation groups.
Container queries own callout behavior when its own width changes.
Cascade layers and semantic tokens provide architecture.

quiz.question: Which layout model best fits a page shell with explicit rows and columns?
quiz.answer: Grid
quiz.explanation: Grid is designed for two-dimensional track relationships.

summary: Plan CSS around responsibilities instead of properties.

lessons.title: Implement and Verify the Portal
lessons.description: Use the reference implementation as a complete target and audit it across responsive and user-preference states.

items: Create semantic HTML for the portal.
Add the layer and token foundation.
Build the page shell with Grid.
Add Flexbox navigation and local groups.
Make the callout region a query container.
Add focus, reduced-motion, and print behavior.
Test narrow, medium, wide, dark, reduced-motion, forced-color, and print states.
Inspect computed styles and remove accidental overflow or specificity problems.

notes.text: The reference project below is complete CSS and HTML rather than a framework abstraction. Students should first attempt the project independently, then compare their architecture and behavior against the reference.

quiz.question: What should progressive enhancement preserve?
options: A usable baseline experience without the optional feature
quiz.answer: A usable baseline experience without the optional feature
quiz.explanation: Enhancements should add capability without making essential content depend on them.

summary: A production CSS project is verified by behavior and maintainability, not only screenshot similarity.

project.name: Accessible Responsive Documentation Portal
project.description: A production-style CSS system for a documentation portal combining semantic styling, responsive Grid and Flexbox, container queries, semantic tokens, color schemes, focus states, reduced motion, print, and progressive enhancement.
steps: Create semantic HTML containing header, navigation, main article, callouts, related links, and footer.
Create the cascade layer order and semantic design tokens.
Apply a minimal reset and readable base typography.
Build the page shell with Grid and a narrow baseline.
Add Flexbox for local navigation groups.
Make the callout region a query container and adapt it with @container.
Add visible keyboard focus and system-aware colors.
Add reduced-motion and print behavior.
Test narrow, medium, wide, dark, print, and accessibility preference states.
Use developer tools to audit matched rules, computed values, layout, and overflow.

CSS guide

Building resilient interfaces with modern CSS

A practical documentation portal demonstrating maintainable CSS architecture, responsive layout, theming, accessibility, and progressive enhancement.

Understanding the cascade

CSS resolves competing declarations through a defined cascade. Layers and low-specificity selectors make that process easier to reason about as a project grows.

Design principle

The component should own its styles while the cascade architecture owns precedence.

Grid

Use Grid when relationships span rows and columns.

Flexbox

Use Flexbox for one-dimensional component arrangements.

Read more

Container queries

Let components respond to the space their container provides.

Read more

Responsive design

Build a useful narrow baseline, then enhance when available space or user preferences warrant a different presentation.

Accessibility

Keep keyboard focus visible, avoid color-only meaning, respect reduced motion, and preserve readability in system color modes.

project.explanation: The project separates reset/base/component/utility concerns with cascade layers. Semantic custom properties form a theme API. Grid controls page-level relationships, Flexbox controls local one-dimensional groups, and container queries make the callout component respond to its own available width. The baseline remains usable without the optional enhancements, while focus-visible, reduced-motion, color-scheme, and print rules adapt the experience to different users and media. Verification should include keyboard-only focus traversal, reduced-motion, light/dark schemes, forced-colors where available, print preview, intermediate widths, and browser support for optional features.
